To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the relationship between the duration of contests and the RHP of the losers is positive, but not for the winners (ii) the relationship between contest escalation and the RHP asymmetry is negative, and (iii) the relationship between mean RHP of a pair and the contest duration is positive.

(i) the duration of animal contests is best explained by models of contest that assume that contestants assess their own RHP; (ii) there is little evidence that the duration of contests is influenced by the occurrence of physical contacts; (iii) the duration of contests in RHP matched rivals can be explained by the mean RHP, but this result should be interpreted with caution; and (iv) there is little consistency between the behaviours observed during contests and the theoretical models that best explain contest duration

(i) contest duration and winner's and loser's RHP are positively correlated in species that settle contests using self assessment; (ii) contest duration is positively correlated with the mean RHP in species that settle contest using mutual assessment; (iii) the relationship between contest escalation and winner RHP is negative; and (iv) there is a weak phylogenetic signal in contest rules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the rules that govern contests between animals.
the question: what rules do animals follow to settle contests?
the question of whether animals follow a single rule or a set of rules to settle contests.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
animals settle contests by using a mix of self and mutual assessment, and this mix varies according to species and context.
WOA and EWOA are the main rules used by animals to settle their contests.
the use of a specific contest model is still a matter of debate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the WOA model, despite its limitations, is still the best available model for predicting contest behaviour.
, in general, animals use self assessment models to settle contests, but they do so in a more complex way than predicted by the models.
the meta-analytic approach is useful to understand how animals solve contests, but that the theoretical framework needs to be expanded to better explain contest outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
contest rules vary among species and that the use of a single theoretical model to explain the evolution of animal contests is unlikely to be successful.
contest rules are not universal and may depend on the ecological and phylogenetic context.
contest rules are not as simple as previously thought.
